Persona Switch: Mixing Distinct Perspectives in Decoding Time

Junseok Kim Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: kim.junseok@snu.ac.kr    Nakyeong Yang Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: yny0506@snu.ac.kr    Kyomin Jung22 2 Corresponding author. Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: kjung@snu.ac.kr
Abstract

Role-play prompting is known to steer the behavior of language models by injecting a persona into the prompt, improving their zero-shot reasoning capabilities. However, such improvements are inconsistent across different tasks or instances. This inconsistency suggests that zero-shot and role-play prompting may offer complementary strengths rather than one being universally superior. Building on this insight, we propose Persona Switch, a novel decoding method that dynamically combines the benefits of both prompting strategies. Our method proceeds step-by-step, selecting the better output between zero-shot and role-play prompting at each step by comparing their output confidence, as measured by the logit gap. Experiments with widely-used LLMs demonstrate that Persona Switch consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 5.13% accuracy improvement. Furthermore, we show that output confidence serves as an informative measure for selecting the more reliable output.11 1 Our code and data have been released on https://github.com/junseokkim00/PersonaSwitch.

1 Introduction

Recent works have explored guiding LLM behavior by assigning personas to the model, known as role-play prompting (Shanahan et al., 2023; Han et al., 2022). This line of studies has suggested that role-play prompting improves language model performance, such as zero-shot reasoning capability, showing empirical observations reveal that the model’s responses can vary depending on the presence of persona (Xu et al., 2023; Kong et al., 2024). Variations in response suggest that the presence of a persona influences the internal representation of the LLM, potentially due to patterns implicitly learned from the model’s training process.

However, subsequent observations indicate that role-play prompting does not always guarantee consistent benefits. This is because prepending a role-play prompt to the context does not contribute essential information that facilitates problem solving. For instance, consider a simple math problem like "What is 4 + 8?". Whether the model receives the question without any persona (zero-shot) or while role-playing as a math teacher, the key information given to the model is unchanged, and the task’s complexity is unaffected either.

To illustrate this, Figure 1 shows the proportion of cases where only one prompting strategy produces the correct answer. The result reveals that the superiority depends on each instance, with neither strategy consistently outperforming the other. Rather, they possess complementary strengths, underscoring the potential of a unified approach that integrates the strengths of both strategies to achieve better performance.

Motivated by these observations, we propose Persona Switch, a novel decoding method that considers both zero-shot and role-play prompting perspectives. Specifically, our method compares the single-step outputs generated from different prompting strategies and selects the more reliable one based on the logit gap. The final response is incrementally constructed by repeating this step-by-step selection process, effectively mixing perspectives of both prompting strategies during decoding. Evaluations on five benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvement, achieving 5.13% of average accuracy gains over the strongest baseline in widely-used LLM. We also find that the logit gap serves as an informative criterion for selecting reliable outputs, leading to improved performance. Furthermore, incorporating only informative tokens to assess output confidence enables more fine-grained selection of reliable outputs, further contributing to performance gains.

2 Related Works

Role-Play Prompting in LLM

Prompting has become a widely used paradigm for adapting language models to various NLP tasks, with zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction-based prompting, showing strong empirical performance (Brown et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021; Kojima et al., 2022). Recent works have explored role-play prompting, where LLMs follow persona-based instructions to simulate specific behaviors (Han et al., 2022; Shanahan et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Kong et al., 2024). These approaches report performance gains across specific tasks, though such benefits are not always consistent or well understood (Zheng et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025). Recent work also highlights that role-play prompting can introduce biases, raising concerns about its robustness and consistent effectiveness across tasks (Salewski et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). Consequently, the inconsistent gains from role-play prompting suggest that it may complement non-role-play strategies, motivating a unified approach that leverages the strengths of both strategies.

3 Methods

3.1 Problem Definition

Role-play prompting is known to effectively steer the model’s behavior by inserting personas into the prompt. However, while adding a persona can change how the model responds, it does not modify the key information available to solve the problem. We define this invariance as the principle of Persona-Agnostic Semantic Invariance.

Persona-Agnostic Semantic Invariance.

Given the same input, introducing a persona does not alter the semantic content of the prompt, thus does not add or remove any task-relevant information.

Therefore, if zero-shot and role-play prompting yield different outputs, there is no basis for claiming that either one is inherently superior. This lack of clear superiority introduces ambiguity when choosing between outputs. To address this, we propose Persona Switch, a decoding method that dynamically selects the better output between zero-shot and role-play prompting at each step, based on the model’s internal confidence signal (logit gap).

3.2 Persona Switch

This section introduces how Persona Switch is executed. Specifically, Persona Switch consists of two steps: Output Candidate Generation and Output Confidence Comparison.

This section describes how to select the final output yfinalty^{t}_{\text{final}} for step tt. We compare their output confidence to select the better one between the two outputs. This approach is motivated by the observation that low-confidence generations are often correlated with incorrect or hallucinated outputs, as suggested by prior studies that analyzed model confidence estimation and generation quality (Kadavath et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Wang and Zhou, 2024). Answer Extraction.

Identifying the exact answer span is challenging. We follow Kojima et al. (2022) by concatenating an answer trigger prompt to elicit only the final answer. The answer trigger prompts for each dataset are in Appendix C.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental setup

Experimental Settings.

We evaluate our method on five widely-used reasoning benchmarks: GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), AQuA-RAT Ling et al. (2017), CSQA Talmor et al. (2019), Last Letter Concatenation Wei et al. (2022) and Tracking Shuffled-Objects from BIG-bench Srivastava et al. (2022)). We use two instruction-tuned variants of the LLaMA-3 family, namely LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, and one from Gemma-2 family, Gemma-2-2B-it, following recent studies demonstrating competitive zero-shot reasoning performance Grattafiori et al. (2024); Team et al. (2024). We compare our method against five baselines (Zero-Shot with Greedy, Top-p, Top-k, Multinomial sampling, and Role-Play Prompting (Kong et al., 2024)), as well as two Persona Switch variants: Low-gap Selection (selects the output with lower average logit gap), and Random Selection (randomly selects between two outputs). Implementation details are in Appendix D.

4.2 Results and analysis

Main Results.

As shown in Table 1, Persona Switch consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Our method achieves the highest overall performance regarding average accuracy, surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.13% and 4.42%, respectively. Furthermore, compared to both low-gap selection and random selection, Persona Switch demonstrates superior accuracy across all datasets, underscoring the efficacy of our logit-based answer selection mechanism. These results validate that selecting responses based on the averaged logit gap yields robust and reliable improvements in multi-domain reasoning tasks.

Analysis of Output Granularity.

Choosing a proper output unit for our method is crucial, as the final response can vary depending on how often outputs of zero-shot and role-play prompting are compared. To assess the impact of output granularity, we evaluated our method at the (1) token, (2) step, and (3) full-sequence level using LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct. Table 3 shows that step-level selection performs best, indicating that evaluating intermediate reasoning steps allows a more diverse integration of zero-shot and role-play perspectives compared to full-sequence selection, leading to improved performance. On the token level, its evaluation tends to underperform as it requires selecting the correct option for every token, where individual tokens lack sufficient context to distinguish the correct reasoning path. Additionally, we also compared confidence using maximum logit, and the consistently better performance of logit gap confirms it as a more informative measure.

Analysis of Filtering Stopwords.

Our approach computes the average logit gap across all tokens when comparing two outputs. However, not all tokens contribute equally to output semantics, as some carry essential information while others, such as stopwords, do not. To assess the impact of removing uninformative tokens, we conduct experiments using two filtering strategies: (1) stopwords, excluding stopwords based on NLTK’s predefined list22 2 https://www.nltk.org/howto/corpus.html, and (2) only numbers, retaining only numerical values. Table 4 shows that applying stopword filtering yields a slight performance gain, suggesting that irrelevant tokens can obscure confidence signals. In contrast, using only numerical tokens degrades performance, likely due to the loss of linguistically meaningful context. Findings suggest that the types of meaningful tokens vary across benchmarks, and applying a task-specific filtering strategy can potentially enhance performance.

Qualitative Analysis.

Table 2 presents several examples from three benchmarks using LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct. In the GSM8K and Last Letter examples, we observe that Persona Switch can produce a better answer when one of the two (zero-shot or role-play prompting) is correct. This demonstrates its ability to identify and favor the more reliable reasoning path. Furthermore, in the Object Tracking example, even when both zero-shot and role-play responses are incorrect, the Persona Switch successfully produces the correct answer by integrating reasoning steps from both outputs. These cases illustrate that the Persona Switch enhances model performance by selectively adopting the better step between the two. Full results for each example can be found in Appendix H.

5 Conclusion

We present Persona Switch, a dynamic decoding strategy that leverages the strengths of both zero-shot and role-play prompting by selecting the better output at each step based on the logit gap. Notably, it can be easily implemented without extra training and shows performance gains compared to using either prompting strategy alone. Ultimately, Persona Switch contributes a simple yet effective decoding-time mechanism, offering a practical framework for integrating distinct prompting strategies.

Limitations

While our method demonstrates promising results, certain limitations suggest potential directions for future work. In our experiments, we adopted fixed role-play prompts from prior studies and used their corresponding datasets, which have a clearly defined ground-truth answer. This setting allowed us to assume persona-agnostic semantic invariance, where the underlying essential information of each input remains consistent regardless of the persona used. However, in more open-ended or subjective tasks where ground-truth answers are inherently ambiguous, the effectiveness of persona-agnostic approaches may vary, motivating further exploration of a framework suited to such settings. Furthermore, our evaluation is limited to zero-shot reasoning tasks. Although our logit-based stepwise selection framework shows strong performance in this context, it remains an open question whether the same approach would be effective in other settings, such as domains beyond reasoning.

Appendix A Dataset-Specific Role-Play Prompts

In our role-play prompting setup, we adopt dataset-specific prompts that were previously designed and validated for task effectiveness by Kong et al. (2024), as shown in Table 5. Each prompt consists of two messages: 1) role-setting prompt, which assigns a specific persona to the LLM through the user message, and 2) role-feedback prompt, which prompts the model to acknowledge its assigned persona by reinforcing the role through the assistant message.

Appendix C Answer Extraction

We extract the final answer by following the method of Kojima et al. (2022). Specifically, we concatenate the output with the dataset-specific answer trigger prompt, triggering the model to only return the answer. Answer trigger prompts for each dataset could be found in Table 6.

Appendix D Baselines and Variants

In this section, we introduce the specific configuration for each baseline used in the main result. We ran the method three times with different seeds (1,2, and 3) and report the average performance.

Greedy decoding

: The model selects the token with the highest probability at each generation. This method is deterministic and often yields fluent but potentially repetitive or overly conservative outputs, as it does not explore alternative candidates.

Top-pp sampling (nucleus sampling)

: This method samples the token from the smallest possible set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a predefined threshold pp. We set p=0.9p=0.9, meaning the model considers a dynamic set of high-probability tokens at each step, encouraging more diverse outputs while maintaining fluency.

Top-kk sampling

: The model restricts sampling to the top kk most probable tokens at each step, and selects one based on their normalized probabilities. We used k=10k=10 in our experiments. This method controls the randomness of generation by limiting the candidate pool, leading to outputs that are both diverse and locally coherent.

Multinomial sampling (temperature sampling)

: This method samples from the full distribution, controlled by a temperature parameter τ\tau. A lower temperature makes the distribution sharper, favoring high-probability tokens, while a higher temperature leads to more randomness. We used τ=0.6\tau=0.6, which is the model’s default value.

Low-gap selection

: As a variant of our method, this approach selects outputs based on the average logit gap between zero-shot and role-play prompting outputs for each step. Specifically, it computes the logit difference for each token and selects the output with the lower average gap.

Random selection

: Another variant of our method, this approach randomly selects between the zero-shot and role-play prompting outputs at each step to construct the final response. This method introduces stochasticity and serves as a baseline for comparison with our method.

Appendix E Dataset Details

In this section, we introduce four different domains, including five distinct datasets used for our experiments. Specific details are shown in Table 7.

Mathematical Reasoning

We use GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), providing math word problems and AQuA-RAT Ling et al. (2017) for multiple choice questions. All questions in this dataset require mathematical reasoning knowledge.

Commonsense Reasoning

We leverage CSQA Talmor et al. (2019), providing multiple choice questions. This dataset requires reasoning based on commonsense knowledge to solve the problem.

Symbolic Reasoning

We use Last Letter Concatenation Wei et al. (2022), which requires concatenating the last letter of the given words in order.

Others

We utilize Tracked Shuffling Objects from Big-Bench Srivastava et al. (2022), which provides a sequence of trading history of the object, and ask for the object’s final position.

Appendix F Impact of Role-Play Prompt design

We conducted additional experiments to evaluate the performance of Persona Switch using multiple variants of the role-play prompt template (Prompts 1, 2, and 3), which differ in verbosity and structure, following Kong et al. (2024). Specifically, Prompt 1 consists solely of the user message, Prompt 2 includes a user–assistant message pair, and Prompt 3 extends Prompt 2 with an additional assistant sentence, which serves as the default in our main experiments. As presented in Table 8, Prompt 3 resulted in the strongest performance across both AQuA and Last Letter tasks. These results suggest that employing a more detailed role-play prompt was associated with improved performance. Based on these findings, we adopted Prompt 3 as the default configuration across all benchmarks.

Appendix G More ablation studies

G.1 Role-Playing vs. Stochastic decoding

To examine whether the performance gains of Persona Switch can be attributed solely to increased decoding diversity, we replace role-playing prompting with standard sampling-based decoding strategies, including top-pp, top-kk, and multinomial sampling, while keeping the rest of the framework unchanged. As shown in Table 9, sampling-based variants consistently underperform Persona Switch on both AQuA and Letter datasets, despite introducing stochastic diversity. This indicates that Persona Switch benefits not merely from sampling multiple candidates within a single output distribution but from role-playing prompts that induce qualitatively distinct reasoning trajectories by shifting the underlying generation distribution, resulting in more coherent and complementary candidate solutions.

Abstract
Role-play prompting is known to steer the behavior of language models by injecting a persona into the prompt, improving their zero-shot reasoning capabilities.
However, such improvements are inconsistent across different tasks or instances.
This inconsistency suggests that zero-shot and role-play prompting may offer complementary strengths rather than one being universally superior.
Building on this insight, we propose Persona Switch , a novel decoding method that dynamically combines the benefits of both prompting strategies.
Our method proceeds step-by-step, selecting the better output between zero-shot and role-play prompting at each step by comparing their output confidence, as measured by the logit gap.
Experiments with widely-used LLMs demonstrate that Persona Switch consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 5.13% accuracy improvement.
Furthermore, we show that output confidence serves as an informative measure for selecting the more reliable output. 1 1

1 Introduction
Recent works have explored guiding LLM behavior by assigning personas to the model, known as role-play prompting ( Shanahan et al., 2023 ; Han et al., 2022 ) .
This line of studies has suggested that role-play prompting improves language model performance, such as zero-shot reasoning capability, showing empirical observations reveal that the model’s responses can vary depending on the presence of persona ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) .
Variations in response suggest that the presence of a persona influences the internal representation of the LLM, potentially due to patterns implicitly learned from the model’s training process.
However, subsequent observations indicate that role-play prompting does not always guarantee consistent benefits.
This is because prepending a role-play prompt to the context does not contribute essential information that facilitates problem solving.
For instance, consider a simple math problem like "What is 4 + 8?" .
Whether the model receives the question without any persona (zero-shot) or while role-playing as a math teacher , the key information given to the model is unchanged, and the task’s complexity is unaffected either.
Figure 1: Relative Correct Rates Show No Clear Superiority Between Prompting Strategies. Each bar represents the proportion of instances where only one strategy answered correctly, highlighting that neither one demonstrates clear superiority.
To illustrate this, Figure 1 shows the proportion of cases where only one prompting strategy produces the correct answer.
The result reveals that the superiority depends on each instance, with neither strategy consistently outperforming the other.
Rather, they possess complementary strengths, underscoring the potential of a unified approach that integrates the strengths of both strategies to achieve better performance.
Motivated by these observations, we propose Persona Switch , a novel decoding method that considers both zero-shot and role-play prompting perspectives.
Specifically, our method compares the single-step outputs generated from different prompting strategies and selects the more reliable one based on the logit gap.
The final response is incrementally constructed by repeating this step-by-step selection process, effectively mixing perspectives of both prompting strategies during decoding.
Evaluations on five benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvement, achieving 5.13% of average accuracy gains over the strongest baseline in widely-used LLM.
We also find that the logit gap serves as an informative criterion for selecting reliable outputs, leading to improved performance.
Furthermore, incorporating only informative tokens to assess output confidence enables more fine-grained selection of reliable outputs, further contributing to performance gains.
2 Related Works
Role-Play Prompting in LLM
Prompting has become a widely used paradigm for adapting language models to various NLP tasks, with zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction-based prompting, showing strong empirical performance ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Wei et al., 2021 ; Kojima et al., 2022 ) .
Recent works have explored role-play prompting, where LLMs follow persona-based instructions to simulate specific behaviors ( Han et al., 2022 ; Shanahan et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) .
These approaches report performance gains across specific tasks, though such benefits are not always consistent or well understood ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) .
Recent work also highlights that role-play prompting can introduce biases, raising concerns about its robustness and consistent effectiveness across tasks ( Salewski et al., 2023 ; Gupta et al., 2023 ) .
Consequently, the inconsistent gains from role-play prompting suggest that it may complement non-role-play strategies, motivating a unified approach that leverages the strengths of both strategies.
3 Methods
3.1 Problem Definition
Role-play prompting is known to effectively steer the model’s behavior by inserting personas into the prompt.
However, while adding a persona can change how the model responds, it does not modify the key information available to solve the problem.
We define this invariance as the principle of Persona-Agnostic Semantic Invariance .
Persona-Agnostic Semantic Invariance.
Given the same input, introducing a persona does not alter the semantic content of the prompt, thus does not add or remove any task-relevant information.
Therefore, if zero-shot and role-play prompting yield different outputs, there is no basis for claiming that either one is inherently superior.
This lack of clear superiority introduces ambiguity when choosing between outputs.
To address this, we propose Persona Switch , a decoding method that dynamically selects the better output between zero-shot and role-play prompting at each step, based on the model’s internal confidence signal (logit gap).

We compare their output confidence to select the better one between the two outputs.
This approach is motivated by the observation that low-confidence generations are often correlated with incorrect or hallucinated outputs, as suggested by prior studies that analyzed model confidence estimation and generation quality ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Wang and Zhou, 2024 ) .

4.1 Experimental setup
Experimental Settings.
We evaluate our method on five widely-used reasoning benchmarks: GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) , AQuA-RAT Ling et al. (2017) , CSQA Talmor et al. (2019) , Last Letter Concatenation Wei et al. (2022) and Tracking Shuffled-Objects from BIG-bench Srivastava et al. (2022) ).
We use two instruction-tuned variants of the LLaMA-3 family, namely LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, and one from Gemma-2 family, Gemma-2-2B-it, following recent studies demonstrating competitive zero-shot reasoning performance Grattafiori et al. (2024) ; Team et al. (2024) .
We compare our method against five baselines (Zero-Shot with Greedy, Top-p, Top-k, Multinomial sampling, and Role-Play Prompting ( Kong et al., 2024 ) ), as well as two Persona Switch variants: Low-gap Selection (selects the output with lower average logit gap), and Random Selection (randomly selects between two outputs).
Implementation details are in Appendix D .
4.2 Results and analysis
Main Results.
As shown in Table 1 , Persona Switch consistently outperforms competitive baselines.
Our method achieves the highest overall performance regarding average accuracy, surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.13% and 4.42%, respectively.
Furthermore, compared to both low-gap selection and random selection, Persona Switch demonstrates superior accuracy across all datasets, underscoring the efficacy of our logit-based answer selection mechanism.
These results validate that selecting responses based on the averaged logit gap yields robust and reliable improvements in multi-domain reasoning tasks.
Analysis of Output Granularity.
Choosing a proper output unit for our method is crucial, as the final response can vary depending on how often outputs of zero-shot and role-play prompting are compared.
To assess the impact of output granularity, we evaluated our method at the (1) token, (2) step, and (3) full-sequence level using LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct.
Table 3 shows that step-level selection performs best, indicating that evaluating intermediate reasoning steps allows a more diverse integration of zero-shot and role-play perspectives compared to full-sequence selection, leading to improved performance.
On the token level, its evaluation tends to underperform as it requires selecting the correct option for every token, where individual tokens lack sufficient context to distinguish the correct reasoning path.
Additionally, we also compared confidence using maximum logit, and the consistently better performance of logit gap confirms it as a more informative measure.

Analysis of Filtering Stopwords.
Our approach computes the average logit gap across all tokens when comparing two outputs.
However, not all tokens contribute equally to output semantics, as some carry essential information while others, such as stopwords, do not.
To assess the impact of removing uninformative tokens, we conduct experiments using two filtering strategies: (1) stopwords , excluding stopwords based on NLTK’s predefined list 2 2

In contrast, using only numerical tokens degrades performance, likely due to the loss of linguistically meaningful context.
Findings suggest that the types of meaningful tokens vary across benchmarks, and applying a task-specific filtering strategy can potentially enhance performance.

Qualitative Analysis.
Table 2 presents several examples from three benchmarks using LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.
In the GSM8K and Last Letter examples, we observe that Persona Switch can produce a better answer when one of the two (zero-shot or role-play prompting) is correct.
This demonstrates its ability to identify and favor the more reliable reasoning path.
Furthermore, in the Object Tracking example, even when both zero-shot and role-play responses are incorrect, the Persona Switch successfully produces the correct answer by integrating reasoning steps from both outputs.
These cases illustrate that the Persona Switch enhances model performance by selectively adopting the better step between the two.
Full results for each example can be found in Appendix H .
5 Conclusion
We present Persona Switch, a dynamic decoding strategy that leverages the strengths of both zero-shot and role-play prompting by selecting the better output at each step based on the logit gap.
Notably, it can be easily implemented without extra training and shows performance gains compared to using either prompting strategy alone.
Ultimately, Persona Switch contributes a simple yet effective decoding-time mechanism, offering a practical framework for integrating distinct prompting strategies.
Limitations
While our method demonstrates promising results, certain limitations suggest potential directions for future work.
In our experiments, we adopted fixed role-play prompts from prior studies and used their corresponding datasets, which have a clearly defined ground-truth answer.
This setting allowed us to assume persona-agnostic semantic invariance, where the underlying essential information of each input remains consistent regardless of the persona used.
However, in more open-ended or subjective tasks where ground-truth answers are inherently ambiguous, the effectiveness of persona-agnostic approaches may vary, motivating further exploration of a framework suited to such settings.
Furthermore, our evaluation is limited to zero-shot reasoning tasks.
Although our logit-based stepwise selection framework shows strong performance in this context, it remains an open question whether the same approach would be effective in other settings, such as domains beyond reasoning.

Appendix D Baselines and Variants
In this section, we introduce the specific configuration for each baseline used in the main result.
We ran the method three times with different seeds (1,2, and 3) and report the average performance.
Greedy decoding
: The model selects the token with the highest probability at each generation. This method is deterministic and often yields fluent but potentially repetitive or overly conservative outputs, as it does not explore alternative candidates.
Top- p p sampling (nucleus sampling)
: This method samples the token from the smallest possible set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a predefined threshold p p . We set p = 0.9 p=0.9 , meaning the model considers a dynamic set of high-probability tokens at each step, encouraging more diverse outputs while maintaining fluency.
Top- k k sampling
: The model restricts sampling to the top k k most probable tokens at each step, and selects one based on their normalized probabilities. We used k = 10 k=10 in our experiments. This method controls the randomness of generation by limiting the candidate pool, leading to outputs that are both diverse and locally coherent.
Multinomial sampling (temperature sampling)
: This method samples from the full distribution, controlled by a temperature parameter τ \tau . A lower temperature makes the distribution sharper, favoring high-probability tokens, while a higher temperature leads to more randomness. We used τ = 0.6 \tau=0.6 , which is the model’s default value.
Low-gap selection
: As a variant of our method, this approach selects outputs based on the average logit gap between zero-shot and role-play prompting outputs for each step. Specifically, it computes the logit difference for each token and selects the output with the lower average gap.
Random selection
: Another variant of our method, this approach randomly selects between the zero-shot and role-play prompting outputs at each step to construct the final response.
This method introduces stochasticity and serves as a baseline for comparison with our method.

Appendix E Dataset Details
In this section, we introduce four different domains, including five distinct datasets used for our experiments. Specific details are shown in Table 7 .
Mathematical Reasoning
We use GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) , providing math word problems and AQuA-RAT Ling et al. (2017) for multiple choice questions. All questions in this dataset require mathematical reasoning knowledge.
Commonsense Reasoning
We leverage CSQA Talmor et al. (2019) , providing multiple choice questions. This dataset requires reasoning based on commonsense knowledge to solve the problem.
Symbolic Reasoning
We use Last Letter Concatenation Wei et al. (2022) , which requires concatenating the last letter of the given words in order.
Others
We utilize Tracked Shuffling Objects from Big-Bench Srivastava et al. (2022) , which provides a sequence of trading history of the object, and ask for the object’s final position.

Appendix G More ablation studies
G.1 Role-Playing vs. Stochastic decoding
To examine whether the performance gains of Persona Switch can be attributed solely to increased decoding diversity, we replace role-playing prompting with standard sampling-based decoding strategies, including top- p p , top- k k , and multinomial sampling, while keeping the rest of the framework unchanged.
As shown in Table 9 , sampling-based variants consistently underperform Persona Switch on both AQuA and Letter datasets, despite introducing stochastic diversity.
This indicates that Persona Switch benefits not merely from sampling multiple candidates within a single output distribution but from role-playing prompts that induce qualitatively distinct reasoning trajectories by shifting the underlying generation distribution, resulting in more coherent and complementary candidate solutions.
